summary: Annika opens by citing a McKinsey Global Institute report showing labor shortages (4.2x/2x jobs-to-people ratio over the past decade) in advanced economies, arguing that AI's next frontier is physical AI for industries like healthcare, construction, and manufacturing. Humanoids adopt human form because the world is built for humans, enabling generalist robots. NVIDIA frames the physical AI lifecycle as a three-computer problem: OVX Omniverse for simulation, DGX for training, and AGX for edge deployment. GR00T N1 is a 2-billion-parameter, open-source, cross-embodiment VLA foundation model announced at GTC. Since no internet-scale robot dataset exists, NVIDIA uses a data pyramid: scarce real teleoperation data at top, synthetic simulation data in the middle, and unstructured internet video at the bottom. DreamGen uses world foundation models to multiply human trajectory data. Aastha details the dual-system architecture inspired by Kahneman's 'Thinking Fast and Slow': System 2 slowly breaks down complex tasks; System 1 executes at ~120 Hz. Inputs are tokenized and processed through a diffusion transformer with an Eagle 2 VLM for vision and text encoding, plus an embodiment-specific action decoder enabling cross-embodiment generalization. Aastha then explains two robot learning paradigms: imitation learning (copying expert demonstrations, bottlenecked by expensive expert data) and reinforcement learning (trial-and-error reward maximization, challenged by the sim-to-real gap). GR00T N1 uses both. Demonstrated tasks include kitchen pick-and-place, a romantic gesture with champagne and flowers, and an industrial pick-and-place with two robots. The talk concludes with three core principles: the data pyramid addressing absent action data, co-training System 1 and System 2 end-to-end (unlike previous independent training that caused disagreement), and a generalist foundation model—likened to Llama—adaptable to any embodiment and downstream task.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation: Physical AI and Labor
sections.summary: Annika introduces herself and Aastha as part of NVIDIA's GR00T N1 team. She presents a McKinsey report showing labor shortages in advanced economies and argues that affected industries (hospitality, healthcare, construction, transportation, manufacturing) require physical AI, not just language models. She explains why humanoids are designed in human form: the world is built for humans.

sections.title: Physical AI Lifecycle and Project GR00T Overview
sections.summary: Describes the three-stage physical AI lifecycle (data generation, model training, edge deployment) and NVIDIA's three-computer problem framing: OVX Omniverse for simulation, DGX for training, AGX for edge. Introduces Project GR00T as NVIDIA's full-stack humanoid robotics strategy, with GR00T N1 as a 2-billion-parameter open-source cross-embodiment foundation model announced at GTC.

sections.title: The Data Pyramid
sections.summary: Explains the data pyramid born of necessity since no internet-scale robot dataset exists. Real teleoperation data is scarce and expensive at the top; synthetic simulation data is in the middle (infinite in theory but labor-intensive); unstructured internet video is at the bottom. Introduces DreamGen (announced at Computex) for multiplying human trajectory data via world foundation models.

sections.title: GR00T N1 Architecture and Dual-System Design
sections.summary: Aastha explains the input/output format, then details the architecture inspired by Kahneman's 'Thinking Fast and Slow': System 2 as slow planner, System 1 as fast executor at ~120 Hz. Describes the pipeline: robot state and noised action encoded into tokens, processed through a diffusion transformer with cross/self-attention, combined with VLM-encoded vision and text tokens (Eagle 2 VLM), and decoded by an embodiment-specific action decoder that enables cross-embodiment generalization.

sections.title: Robot Learning Methods and Conclusion
sections.summary: Aastha elaborates on the action decoder's role in cross-embodiment generalization, then introduces two robot learning paradigms: imitation learning (copying expert demonstrations, minimizing loss against a gold standard, but bottlenecked by expensive expert data) and reinforcement learning (trial-and-error reward maximization without a gold standard, but challenged by the sim-to-real gap). GR00T N1 uses both. Demonstrated tasks include kitchen pick-and-place, a romantic gesture, and an industrial task with two robots. The talk concludes with three core principles: the data pyramid (no internet-scale action data), co-trained dual-system architecture (unlike previous independent training causing disagreement), and a generalist model—likened to Llama—adaptable to any embodiment and downstream task.

limitations: No internet-scale robot dataset exists—robots haven't made it to YouTube
Real teleoperation data is very small in quantity and expensive to collect
High-quality simulation environments are labor-intensive to create and require serious skill
Sensors don't capture actions perfectly, resulting in noised actions
Imitation learning is severely bottlenecked by expensive expert data
Reinforcement learning faces a significant sim-to-real gap, an active area of research
Previously, training System 1 and System 2 independently caused disagreement between the two systems
quantitativeClaims: McKinsey report shows 4.2x/2x ratio of jobs to available workers over the past decade in the 30 most advanced economies
GR00T N1 is a 2-billion-parameter model, described as tiny by LLM standards but sizable for robotics
Real teleoperation data collection is nominally 24 hours per robot per day but less in practice due to human and robot fatigue
